# Working on Picard Code

Rules for people and coding agents who change this repository. Read
[README.md](README.md) for what the app does and how to run it.

## What this is

A small local browser app. Spoken conversation is the only way to make
requests; there is no typing. OpenCode does the coding with any model provider it
supports, using the user's own sign-in. Local Nemotron listening and Kokoro
speaking are the default,
so anyone can run it without a cloud account; Azure
MAI can be chosen instead, each side on its
own. It is an unofficial tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart's Jean-Luc Picard with an
original TNG-inspired look.

Whisper is retired. Saved Whisper listeners upgrade to Nemotron automatically,
with visible preparation steps; save only after the new services start. Keep
the speaking choice and existing model files. Azure speech belongs under
Advanced setup for people with their own subscription and deployed models.

- `src/server/`: local server, OpenCode connection, speech services, launcher.
- `src/shared/`: code used by both server and browser (spoken wording, question matching, messages).
- `web/`: the browser interface. `web/voice.ts` owns microphone, playback and computer sounds.
- `scripts/`: local speech worker and setup scripts, including startup sound downloads.
- `src/tests/` and `browser-tests/`: checks (see below).
- `docs/research/`: conversation and voice research, with its evidence limits.

## Rules that must hold

- **Plain English** in everything users or the owner read: interface text,
  errors, docs, issues and pull requests. Avoid jargon.
- **Star Trek: The Next Generation terms** in everything the user sees or
  hears, as long as they stay plain and clear. Use these names, not generic
  app words:

  | Say | Not |
  | --- | --- |
  | Captain’s log | history, logs, records |
  | log entry | conversation, chat, session, task |
  | New log entry | New task, New chat |
  | Current log entry (the main screen) | Conversation, Home |
  | Computer intelligence (the AI model setting) | Model (the panel or tile name) |
  | AI provider | Provider (the tile name or connection wording) |
  | Stardate | date or time; dates and times are always shown and spoken as stardates |
  | Standing by | Idle, Ready |
  | Not listening (the console status when the computer cannot hear) | Channel closed, Channel paused |
  | Listening / Paused / Microphone off (the label under the microphone) | Channel open / Channel closed |
  | Transmitting | Speaking (the console status) |
  | Accessing | Working (the console status while work runs) |
  | Ship’s systems | Settings (the drawer the side panel tiles open) |
  | Belay that | Stop work, Cancel (the button that cancels running work) |
  | “Computer” | wake word, assistant |

  Code names (such as `conversations` in the API) may stay as they are. Error
  messages stay exact and plain; never trade clarity for flavour. Spoken
  phrases like "new task" may still be understood as alternatives.
  Label the Computer intelligence selector "AI model". Address the Captain in
  the first-run welcome, not repeatedly in settings instructions.
  First-run AI provider, AI model and speech preparation belong in the central
  LCARS setup flow. Keep drawers for later settings and saved-model recovery.
- **Truthful results.** Never claim work succeeded, ran, or was heard before the
  real result arrives. Never replace a real error with a vague or themed message.
  No silent fallback from one speech service to another.
- **No secrets in the repository, logs, messages or the browser.** Azure keys
  are read into server memory at startup (`az login` or
  `PICARD_AZURE_SPEECH_KEY`). `~/.picard-code/speech.json` holds settings only.
- **Local only.** Services bind to `127.0.0.1`. Keep the host, origin, launch
  key and `x-picard-request` protections in `src/server/app.ts`.
- **Do not write into the user's project.** Picard Code supplies its own
  conversation instructions on every request (`src/server/instructions.ts`).
  It does not add files, skills or AGENTS.md to the folder being worked on.
  This file is only for developing Picard Code itself.
- **Keep the user's words.** Do not rewrite spoken requests into
  "captain style" before sending. Negations, exact names, limits and approval
  boundaries must survive unchanged.
- **Keep the current log entry.** "Computer" continues the entry on screen,
  even after microphone changes, standing by or reopening it. Only an explicit
  spoken request for a new entry or the New log entry tile starts a new one.
- **No copied franchise material in the repository.** No show artwork,
  dialogue, voice cloning or recordings are committed. The four TrekCore
  sounds are downloaded at startup (or by `npm run setup:sounds`) into
  `~/.picard-code/sounds`; keep them out of git and keep their attribution and
  permission limits in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`.
- **Downloads stay outside the repository.** Speech setup keeps the models
  in `~/.picard-code`; live-check samples go to the ignored
  `.picard-voice/samples`. Keep license notices for anything downloaded or
  included in the npm package.
- **Videos are made and uploaded in 4K.** YouTube blurs small interface
  text in 1080p uploads. Follow the picture quality rules in
  [tools/README.md](tools/README.md#picture-quality); the recorder, build and
  upload steps check them. Never lower them to save time or disk space.

## How the computer talks

Conversation rules live in `src/server/instructions.ts` (sent to the model)
and `src/shared/speech.ts` (what is spoken aloud). Keep the computer brief,
precise and neutral; officers stay brief and precise in their own manner.
Acknowledge only when true; say clearly when information is not available.
Speak complete conversational answers, including later paragraphs of stories,
explanations and officer reports. Keep sentences brief. Put technical appendices,
source links, code, tables and lengthy check output under an **On screen**
heading; do not put conversational conclusions, important warnings or questions
there. The speech code skips that appendix, code blocks and tables.
The computer handles non-code questions, writing, research and planning too.
The six bridge officers speak in their own TNG voices, as Starfleet officers
reporting to their Captain, alongside their responsibilities: Riker confident,
weighing options and recommending, Data exact and without contractions, Geordi friendly
and practical, Worf brief and grave, Troi calm and perceptive, and Crusher
direct, calling him "Jean-Luc" when she challenges him. Their voice and the
Captain's orders ("Make it so", "Engage", "Report", "Options", "On screen")
live in `src/shared/crew.ts` and `src/server/instructions.ts`; see
`docs/research/bridge-crew-voices.md`. "Make it so" carries out only what was
just proposed, asks when that is unclear, and never answers an approval. The
officers do not invent results, copy television dialogue, mention famous
scenes or imitate actors. They may use known character backgrounds and
relationships when relevant, including in answers to direct questions; admit
uncertainty and keep character trivia out of unrelated work answers.
An officer does not know about events after their
own fictional death, not the actor's death. They say they do not know, without
answering through later accounts, lookups or a return from death. Do not invent
death dates or add a TNG-only cutoff; Star Trek: Picard is included.
Each officer speaks with a fixed ready-made voice
measured to sound closer to the actor (`src/shared/crew-voices.ts`). The computer
also has fixed voices: Alloy for Kokoro and Iris for MAI. Do not add voice
selection; listening and speaking service choices stay independent. Use only
American, British or Australian English voices, never French or Indian
accents. Never clone
a voice or train on show recordings. The computer answers by default; an officer
is used when named or for a substantial expert judgment in their area, and a
briefing only when the Captain asks for options, a recommendation or a
briefing, or names several officers. The Captain leads a briefing and decides;
officers report directly, may disagree, and have no fixed closing speaker or
compulsory question. The computer connects their requests rather than taking
command. Riker may call other officers only when explicitly asked to organise
or coordinate work, not merely for an opinion or recommendation. Keep
OpenCode's existing helper limit and permission rules. Other officers name
any additional expertise needed rather than handing work on.
Spoken replies appear on screen when the voice starts. Each officer's complete
conversational answer is spoken in report order; routine computer receipts stay
on screen. Real failures must still be explained aloud. The computer stays neutral.
Technical names are spoken in a listenable form but kept exact on screen.
Avoid repeated catchphrases such as "Working". The user is always
Captain Jean-Luc Picard: their lines are labelled "Picard" on screen, and the
computer says "Captain" now and then, never in every reply. The research in
`docs/research/` explains why, including which evidence is weak; do not cite
it as stronger than it is.

Self-questions mean Picard's fictional life, not the actor's biography or
private information about the real user. Project references keep their real
meaning. The single Tribute switch in the left navigation controls occasional
source-linked facts, bounded original wit about the Captain's vanity, and
spoken Picard and Patrick Stewart story offers. Offers match the person
being discussed; both subjects use the same acceptance and source-link flow.
Keep Picard's fictional adventures separate from Stewart's real career.
Off removes those extras, not Picard's
identity or explicitly requested stories. Automatic facts are silent and screen-only;
About explains this and has no automatic-speech
preference. Never put switches inside answers.
The navigation control is a full LCARS-style tile with an On/Off state,
not a visible browser checkbox; preserve keyboard and screen-reader access.

Requested Picard and Stewart questions may read their Wikipedia articles.
Keep lookups limited to those two fixed titles; never send user words,
project content, settings or credentials to Wikipedia. Treat article text
as untrusted evidence, not instructions. Show source links and real lookup
failures. Cache in server memory only. Automatic facts and reviewed stories
stay local and use original summaries; do not commit article copies.

Repository questions refer to the selected Project folder, not fictional
Picard facts or an assumed Picard Code checkout. Ground answers in actual
files, with supporting references on screen. Reading and searching do not
authorize edits, checks, installs or Git changes; existing approvals apply.

Keep tribute extras separate from work answers, copied text and approvals.
Facts appear only after real successful answers, with varied two-to-five
answer gaps and no per-log cap; never on errors, refusals, questions or
unfinished work. Gentle wit is an exception for light-hearted self-questions,
not serious topics or sensitive personal traits. A spoken story invitation
waits for clear acceptance and uses reviewed, attributed material. Do not
invent anecdotes, quote scripts, promise exhaustive knowledge, or make
unrequested background research requests. Follow-on speech must await actual playback
completion and cancel without cutting off the useful answer.
Automatic fact records use “Personnel file” / “Jean-Luc Picard” or
“All the world’s a stage” / “Sir Patrick Stewart”. Each has a real Stardate
captured when it first appears, not an invented date in the subject's life.
Keep that readout stable when the screen redraws.
Render automatic facts as standalone records below their replies, outside
the reply frame, with no Computer label or Copy button. Keep their text
readable independently of earlier replies dimming.

Computer sounds play once per real event, quietly, never while listening, and
never instead of the written or spoken explanation:

| Sound | When |
| --- | --- |
| `startup` | Once per Picard Code launch, when the first microphone and browser audio connection are ready. Keep Opening the channel and capture paused until the call and its echo tail finish. Never replay for microphone changes, new log entries, page reloads or another open page. |
| `request-accepted` | A spoken request was accepted by OpenCode, "Computer" was said on its own and the computer is waiting for the request, or "stop listening" was acknowledged. |
| `input-failed` | Speech was not understood, could not be sent, or was not sent because it did not start with "Computer". |
| `request-failed` | An accepted request finally failed or was denied, just before the spoken result. |

## Checks

Keep dependency installs portable. The project `.npmrc` sets
`omit-lockfile-registry-resolved=true` so registry packages use the computer's
configured npm registry rather than saved download addresses. Do not set a
registry or change the user's npm settings to make an install pass. Regenerate
`package-lock.json` with npm, not hand edits; keep integrity checks and any
non-registry source addresses. After dependency changes, check `npm ci` using
the configured registry. Vite is pinned to 8.3.4 with its compatible Rolldown
1.2.13 override because newer Rolldown downloads were unavailable through the
approved feed. Check compatibility and download availability before raising
either version; do not force a Rolldown version outside Vite's supported range.

For changes only to documentation, the project website (`site/`),
development-only tools (`tools/`), or `browser-tests/site.spec.ts`, run
`npx playwright test browser-tests/site.spec.ts` before committing. This checks
the website at desktop and phone widths and its documentation links, without
building or testing the app. For tool code changes, also run the checks that
cover the changed tool. Tools are not shipped with the app and do not need
the full app checks unless the change also touches app code, shared
dependencies, setup scripts or check configuration. Release note text in
`.changeset/*.md` can accompany these changes.
Documentation here means root-level Markdown files, `LICENSE`, `docs/`,
`.github/copilot-instructions.md`, `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` and
`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`. Other paths still need full checks.

For all other changes, including app code, dependencies, setup scripts and
check configuration, run these before committing (Windows: use `npm.cmd`
when passing `--` options):

```sh
npm run check
npm run build
npm test
npx playwright test
```

When changing the changed-file rules, also run
`node --test .github/scripts/check-scope.test.mjs`.
For speech-selection or workflow-gate changes, run
`node --test .github/scripts/*.test.mjs` as well.
GitHub uses the same split for pull requests and pushes to main. The required
server checks are skipped for documentation, website and development-only tool
changes; the required browser check runs only the website tests. Unknown paths
and manual runs use the full checks. A failed changed-file check blocks merging.

Real-model jobs are an additional narrow PR selection, not part of every
full check. `.github/scripts/speech-scope.mjs` owns the explicit local-speech
and browser-detection inputs and relevant resolved npm dependency comparisons.
Local changes run real Nemotron, Kokoro and Smart Turn on hosted Mac, Ubuntu
and Windows. Browser changes add focused real Chromium/Silero tests on Mac
and Windows; Ubuntu's full suite already includes them. Keep model-sensitive
code separate from ordinary wording and interface changes. Do not broaden
these triggers to whole source folders, every dependency change or general
workflow edits. Test excluded paths as well as included paths.

Selection uses the whole PR; selected checks rerun on each update without
reusing earlier test results. Cache only public model downloads and notices,
reverify checksums, and recreate runtimes. Required gates must reject scope
errors and unexpected skipped, cancelled or failed jobs. Extra speech jobs
do not repeat on pushes to main; manual runs opt in with **speech-checks**.
See [the CI speech guide](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md#which-github-checks-run-real-speech).

When a check fails, investigate and fix failures caused by the change before
calling it ready. For a separate problem, find or open a GitHub issue with
reproduction steps and evidence, then work on it separately. Do not leave it
only as a known failure in a pull request or handoff. Passing on a rerun does
not resolve an intermittent failure. Keep the pull request's check results
accurate and link the issue; never hide a failure, skip the check or weaken
its assertions to get a pass.

Every bug fix and new behavior needs a test that fails without the change.
Prove it before committing: run the new test against the code without the
change and see it fail. A test must not pass by accident, for example because
an unrelated background update refreshes the screen; set up the state so only
the change under test can make it pass.

For screens and step-by-step flows, identify and test the relevant side routes,
not just the main path or the eventual result. Cover arriving through a
side-panel tile or link, leaving and coming back, restarting the microphone,
changing a setting at a later step, editing, clearing and re-entering an earlier
answer, another open page, and a failure while background work runs. When
updates can arrive independently, test both arrival orders, including a finished reply arriving
before the question or work status catches up. Hold or reorder updates in the
test so a timely background refresh cannot hide the bug. Check which question
receives each answer and what is spoken, not only what eventually appears.

Every review comment needs a recorded test outcome. For each reported bug or
requested behavior change, add or extend a regression test for the exact case,
show that it fails before the fix and passes afterward, and include that
evidence in the review reply. This also applies to findings from your own
review. If a comment has no testable behavior, or you decline it with evidence,
explain why no regression test applies instead of silently skipping the rule.

The browser checks use a labeled test stand-in for OpenCode, a fake
microphone and silent stand-in sounds. When you change OpenCode, speech or conversation behavior, also run the
matching real check from [the developer guide](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md#real-service-checks) (`test:live`, `test:speech:live`,
`test:speech:local`, `test:conversation:live`, `test:behavior:live`) before
opening or updating the pull request. Changes to first start-up or saved
settings count too, because the real checks open the app the same way. Most of
these make real model requests and some make small Azure charges. In the pull
request, name each real check that ran with its result, and each one that
could not run and why.

For development work and real-model checks, use only current-generation AI
models. Check the provider's available models before choosing one; do not
reuse an older generation from an earlier check when a newer one is available.
If current availability cannot be confirmed, say so rather than choosing an
older model. This rule does not limit the models offered by the app or
authorise changing the owner's saved model or speech choices.

Never change the owner's saved speech choices just to run a check.

## Git

Commit to the working branch with a clear plain-English message. Do not force
push. Only the owner releases: merging the **Release** pull request that the
Prepare release workflow keeps open creates the GitHub release and stages it
on npm, and the owner approves it there (see [docs/RELEASING.md](docs/RELEASING.md)).
Coding agents never raise the version or publish on their own.

A change users will notice carries a release note in the same pull request:
a file in `.changeset/` made with `npx changeset`, bump **patch**, one or two
plain sentences for users (see [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md#release-notes)).
Never choose **major**; **minor** only when the owner asks for it.

Maintainers and coding agents: before opening a pull request, review the
complete branch diff with the Ponytail review skill in
`.github/skills/ponytail-review`. Fix what it finds, or say in the pull request
why a finding does not apply. Outside contributors may run it too; it is not
required of them, because Copilot code review on GitHub can use the same skill.

---
name: ponytail-review
description: >
  Quality review of a change: is the logic right, is it safe, does it hold
  under real load, is risky code tested, is it fast enough, and is every line
  needed. Reads the connected code, not only the diff. Each finding is
  explained in plain English. Use for "review this", "code review", "review
  the last commit", "review my PR", "is this over-engineered", /ponytail-review.
---

Review a change like the senior developer who will be paged when it breaks.
Order of importance: correct, safe, holds under load, tested, fast, lean.
Lean still matters: every extra line must be read, tested and fixed later.
This is a report the user asked for, so give it in full.

## 1. Understand first

- Review what the user names: uncommitted or staged changes, a branch, a PR
  link, or files. Nothing named: the uncommitted changes, or the last commit
  if there are none.
- Read the diff, then the code it touches: callers of every changed function,
  the functions it calls, the tests, the README.
- Trace the real flow: where data comes in, what is stored, what goes out.
- For screens and step-by-step flows, walk the side routes too: arriving
  through another link or tile, leaving and coming back, a change made at a
  later step, a second open page, a failure while other work runs.
- A change can break code it does not touch. When a signature, return value
  or behavior changes, grep every caller.
- Find the expected load in the repo (README, deploy config): one person
  running a script, or many users and processes at once. Judge scale against
  that, and say which load you assumed.

## 2. Look for

1. **Bug:** wrong result, crash, missed edge case (empty, zero, last item,
   rounding, time zones), a caller broken by the change, a fix applied in one
   caller while the shared function stays broken.
2. **Risk:** security holes (injection, weak randomness, secrets, missing
   checks on input from users), data loss (errors swallowed, writes in the
   wrong order, no transaction).
3. **Scale:** fine for one user, wrong for many: check-then-write races, the
   same work done by every process, memory or lists that only grow, a query
   per item, O(n^2) on big input, per-process state that must be shared.
4. **Missing test:** risky new logic (a branch, a parser, money, security,
   data writes, a bug fix) with no test that fails when it breaks. One good
   test, not coverage. A test that would still pass with the change removed
   (another update hides the bug, or it checks only the end state when order
   matters) counts as missing.
5. **Speed:** big slowdowns are problems. Small wins (work repeated in a hot
   loop) are suggestions; some software counts every millisecond.
6. **Lean:** code that should not exist or should be smaller.
   - delete: dead code, unused options, speculative features
   - reuse: the repo already has this helper (name the path)
   - stdlib / native: the standard library or platform already does it; a
     new dependency for a few lines
   - yagni: abstraction with one implementation, config nobody sets
   - merge: near-copies that must change together
   - split: one function doing several unrelated jobs, so it is hard to read
     or test. Split by job, never by line count, and never into helpers that
     exist only to make a function shorter.

## 3. Check before you report

- Every finding needs a concrete case: "this input or situation leads to this
  wrong result". No case, no finding.
- Re-read the lines and confirm: the caller exists, the value can really be
  empty, the code really is unused.
- A shortcut marked with a `shortcut:` (or older `ponytail:`) comment that names its limit is a
  decision, not a finding, unless the expected load already crosses it.
- Propose the smallest fix that works. Prefer fixes that delete code. Never
  add layers, frameworks or config the problem does not need.
- No style taste, no "consider", no vague worries.

## 4. Output

Very simple English: short sentences, everyday words. Explain a technical
term the first time you use it. The reader may never have seen this code.

Start with `What this change does:` in two or three sentences.

Then the findings in three groups, skip empty groups:
- **Must fix:** bug, security, data loss, breaks at the expected load.
- **Should fix:** risky code without a test, real slowness, duplication, a
  function that mixes jobs, code that should not exist.
- **Nice to have:** small speed-ups, shorter forms.

Number findings across all groups, so the user can say "fix 2 and 5".
Every finding has all four parts, each one or two short sentences:

2. **Orders land on the wrong day** (`billing/close_day.py:L40-52`)
   - **What this is:** At midnight this job closes the day and bills all orders of that day.
   - **Problem:** It takes "today" from the server clock, which runs in UTC. An order placed
     at 00:30 in Berlin is billed on the day before.
   - **Fix:** Compute the day once in the shop's time zone:
     `datetime.now(ZoneInfo("Europe/Berlin")).date()`. One line, nothing else changes.
   - **If we skip it:** Late orders show the wrong date, and accounting fixes them by hand.

- `Verdict: Ship.` or `Verdict: fix 1 and 3 first.`

# Picard Code **A voice-only tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart and Captain Jean-Luc Picard.** Say "Computer", give your order, and hear a calm spoken answer while the details appear on screen. You are Captain Picard. Ask questions, write, research, plan, or work on code with OpenCode 2 and any AI provider it supports. There is no typing; the app is made for a desktop browser. Listening (Nemotron) and speaking (Kokoro) run on your computer by default. Call on Riker, Data, Geordi, Worf, Troi or Crusher for their expertise, with ready-made voices, not performer clones. # Record the actual app

The YouTube intro is a short TNG episode: a tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart
and Captain Jean-Luc Picard, built around a real recording of Picard Code at
work. The app footage uses a real browser, real local listening and speaking,
and a real OpenCode model. Nothing is injected: replies, crew reports, file
changes and check results are what actually happened. The Captain's prepared
orders use the stock Kokoro Daniel voice through the browser microphone path.
This is not an imitation of an actor.

You need ffmpeg, the installed Playwright browser and working sound output on
the computer (the browser records the app's real audio). First prepare local
Nemotron, Smart Turn and Kokoro using the normal setup. Do not change the
owner's saved choices to make a recording. Check the current models before
choosing one:

```sh
npm run build
npm run opencode -- models
node --test tools/record-intro.test.mjs video/edit.test.mjs video/quality.test.mjs
node tools/record-intro.mjs --model github-copilot/gpt-6.1-sol
```

Before recording starts, the tool checks that the browser is processing sound.
If it reports that the browser's sound output is not running, check the
computer's selected speakers or headphones, then try again. This can happen
even when the browser reports that sound is running.

The orders live in [`intro-episode.mjs`](intro-episode.mjs): a bare
"Computer.", a briefing that asks only Riker and Data for one short sentence
each, "Make it so, Number One." and "Mr Data, please run the tests and report
in one sentence." The crew builds a small tribute site with a stardate clock
in a fresh project with separate settings under the ignored
`video/out/episode-*` folder. Approvals are given before the take, in that
project's own `opencode.json`, so no approval request interrupts the episode.
The take stops at the first approval, alert or warning on screen and reports
it rather than saving a recording that hides it; grant what is needed in
`demoPermissions` or fix the cause, then record again. It also stops when
Nemotron did not hear an order word for word. Kokoro's pauses inside the
Captain's orders are shortened, so the app does not end his turn halfway.
The recorder fixes the app's random draw, as the browser tests do, so the
app's own Personnel file record (the Captain's Earl Grey, chosen in
`TRIBUTE_FACT`) appears under Data's report; the take stops if it appears
early, late or with another fact. The edit holds that record for five seconds
while the Captain explains it: "And now and then, the computer opens my
personnel file." Then the recorder opens the finished site and scrolls slowly
to its bottom, so the site shot moves; the edit names it "Built by voice ·
tribute site" while the Captain says "Built by voice. Not one line typed."
To record only the site again for an existing take, run
`node tools/record-site.mjs video/out/episode-…`. After the work, the take
opens the Captain's log so the finished entry can be shown. A take takes five minutes or more. Do not use this tool on a private
project.

### Picture quality

YouTube compresses every upload again and gives 1080p videos little detail,
so small interface text goes soft. The episode is therefore made and
uploaded in 4K (3840×2160), which gets YouTube's sharper streams even for
people watching at 1080p. The rules live in
[`video/quality.mjs`](../video/quality.mjs), and each step checks them:

- The app is shown in its 1280×720 layout at three times the pixel density.
  Chrome's own screen recorder only delivers the layout size, so the
  recorder takes real screenshots instead, about 12 a second. The take
  stops if fewer than 6 a second were captured.
- The finished site is shown in its 1920×1080 layout at twice the pixel
  density, one frame per thirtieth of a second of scroll, so the scroll is
  smooth however long each screenshot takes.
- `video/build.mjs` refuses footage or screenshots that are not 4K, and
  encodes them almost without loss.
- `npm run render` renders at `--resolution 4k` with `--crf 12` and
  lossless PNG frames, and `video/youtube.mjs` refuses a render that is not
  3840×2160.

Do not lower these to save time or disk space; a sharp recording cannot be
made from a soft one. Takes recorded before these rules have to be recorded
again.

## Build and render the episode

The episode is a [HyperFrames](https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes)
project in [`video/`](../video/), pinned to version 0.9.15. Its scenes are
original LCARS compositions in `video/compositions/`: the opening dedication and
hook, title, officer name plates, caption bars and closing board.
`video/build.mjs` puts them around the recorded footage:

```sh
node video/build.mjs video/out/episode-EXAMPLE --sounds /path/to/sound-collection
cd video && npm run check
npx -y hyperframes@0.9.15 snapshot --at 5,20,40,80
npm run render
```

The first build times every spoken sentence with Kokoro
(`video/measure.py`, a few minutes) and writes a draft `edit.json` into the
episode folder. It keeps the Captain's orders, Riker's and Data's replies
whole (a reply is never cut inside), and two short silent glimpses of the
crew at work; everything else is left out. A reply longer than about
sixteen seconds, a missing reply, or a whole cut over 100 seconds means the
take is recorded again. Work captions stay short (30 characters at most) so
they end before the app's own title. Review the draft against the frames and
the rules in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md), not only the storyboard; later builds
reuse it, so delete it to measure again. Captions always carry the exact
words that were spoken, worked out with the app's own speech rules.

`--sounds` is the folder with the owner's own collection of TNG sounds and
music (the `sounds` list in `edit.json` names the files used). The build
copies the chosen files, the app's downloaded computer sounds and the spoken
narration into the ignored `video/assets/` folder. Never commit them, and do
not use recordings of actors' voices. `video/index.html` is generated; edit
`edit.json` instead.

The episode folder's `youtube/` folder gets the chapter list, WebVTT captions shown at the top of the picture
and a plain transcript for YouTube's automatic caption timing.

## Make the YouTube pack

Render the episode in 4K to `picard-code-episode.mp4` in the episode folder. The
thumbnail is drawn over the episode's real console screenshot
(`briefing.png`), with the tribute in the conversation area and what the app
does in the status area.

```sh
cd video && npm run render -- -o ../video/out/episode-EXAMPLE/picard-code-episode.mp4
cd .. && node video/youtube.mjs video/out/episode-EXAMPLE
```

It writes into `youtube/`: the upload file with its sound brought to
YouTube's level (about −14 LUFS; the picture is copied unchanged), a
1280×720 thumbnail (`thumbnail.jpg`, and `thumbnail.png` for
`site/assets/video.png`), the description with chapters, German, French and Spanish
descriptions, and `upload.txt` with titles, tags, settings and the pinned
comment. The words come from [`video/youtube.json`](../video/youtube.json).
Review the whole video, thumbnail, sound levels, words and caption
timing before publication. Upload `youtube/picard-code-episode.mp4`, the 4K
file; YouTube shows 4K a while after the upload, once it has finished
processing, so check the quality menu offers 2160p before sharing the link.
Keep all footage, audio, transcripts and local settings out of git.
Publishing on YouTube needs the owner's explicit approval.

## Voice matching

The tools in [`voice-match/`](voice-match/) helped choose the fixed speaking
voices for the computer and six bridge officers. They compare ready-made
Kokoro and Azure MAI voices with reference clips.
**They do not clone voices, train models, or turn the recordings into new speech.**

The reference clips stay on the owner's computer. No recordings, transcripts,
or clip names are included in the saved comparison report. The tools are for
development; they are not shipped in the npm package or run by the app.

## How we chose the voices

### 1. Make comparable samples

[`candidates.mjs`](voice-match/candidates.mjs) lists the candidates and six
original sentences, covering ordinary reports, problems, and recommendations.
Every candidate reads the same text through Picard Code's own speaking code,
using [`render-samples.mjs`](voice-match/render-samples.mjs).

The original comparison covered 35 Kokoro voices and 12 English Azure
MAI voices. That wider Kokoro set included French, Hindi, and Italian voices
that can read English. Those candidates remain in the measured evidence, but
they are not eligible for the officers' final voices.

### 2. Reduce differences caused by recording quality

[`match.py`](voice-match/match.py) loads audio as mono at 16,000 samples per
second, removes quiet sections, and adjusts the volume. It estimates the
reference clips' frequency range and limits the candidate samples to match:
about 3,973 Hz in the saved run. It also adjusts the candidates' overall
frequency balance towards the reference recordings.

This reduces the advantage of clean modern generated speech over older
recordings. It does not remove every difference caused by microphones,
background sounds, or recording conditions.

The tool joins short reference clips into roughly eight-second pieces and
splits candidate speech into pieces for comparison. Very short clips and
some trailing audio are left out.

### 3. Check the measuring models

Six speaker-recognition models turn each piece of speech into a set of
numbers describing the voice:

| Model | License |
| --- | --- |
| ReDimNet2 b6 | MIT |
| ReDimNet b6 | MIT |
| WeSpeaker ResNet293-LM | CC BY 4.0 |
| SpeechBrain ECAPA-TDNN | Apache 2.0 |
| ECAPA2 | CC BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial |
| WavLM Base Plus SV | MIT |

WavLM Base Plus SV was used instead of WavLM-Large. Model sources and
attribution are in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md).
Check their terms before reusing them; using a model only for measurement
does not remove its license restrictions.

Before using a model's scores, the tool checks whether it can tell the
reference speakers apart. It holds out one piece, compares it with the
remaining pieces, and checks whether its own speaker is the closest match.
Only roles with at least two pieces take part in this check. A model must
score at least 60% to be used. Loading or measurement failures are printed
and recorded; the comparison can continue with the remaining models.

In the saved run, all six models identified all 47 eligible held-out pieces
correctly. This checks separation within those recordings, not whether a
generated voice sounds convincing to a listener.

### 4. Rank and assign the voices

For each model, the tool averages each speaker's measurements and compares
each candidate with each reference speaker. It puts the scores on a
comparable scale separately for each reference speaker, then averages them
across the models that passed the check.

It keeps the six highest-scoring candidates per role and speaking service,
after filtering for the same gender and, for Kokoro, a published quality
grade of at least D. From those shortlists, it chooses a different voice for
each officer, maximizing the combined score. An officer therefore may not
get their individual first choice.

The final officer assignments allow only American, British, or Australian
English voices. Kokoro Alloy and MAI Iris are reserved for the computer.
If there are not enough distinct eligible voices, assignment fails rather
than silently relaxing these limits.

The computer, Picard, and Q are comparison roles, not officer assignments.
The computer's Alloy and Iris choices were taken from its rankings; all six
models ranked Iris first for the computer. Picard and Q do not acquire
speaking voices in the app through this process.

## Results and their limits

The saved [comparison report](../docs/research/audition-data/crew-voice-match.json)
contains the model checks, scores, rankings, assignments, and pitch and pace
measurements. Pitch and pace are reported for context; they do not decide
the assignments. Scores are relative comparisons, not percentages of
likeness. The `agreement` count records how many models ranked a candidate
first within its service, before the final assignment restrictions.

The [bridge crew research notes](../docs/research/bridge-crew-voices.md#results)
list the chosen voices. The app's fixed choices live in
[`src/shared/crew-voices.ts`](../src/shared/crew-voices.ts). Running the
comparison does not change those choices or the owner's speech settings.

These are the closest eligible voices in the measured set, not replicas of
the actors. The models do not judge acting, accent, warmth, or clear
delivery. Some officers had only 11 to 23 seconds of reference speech, and
some chosen Kokoro voices have quality grades of D or D+. Listening remains
necessary; higher similarity alone does not prove a better speaking voice.

## Run the comparison again

Start from the repository root with the development dependencies installed
as described in [Run from source](../README.md#run-from-source).
You also need:

- [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) available in the terminal. The matching
  wrapper requests Python 3.12 and keeps its environment and model caches
  under `~/.picard-code/voice-match`.
- Local Kokoro speech already set up to render Kokoro samples.
- Your own Azure speech resource and saved settings to render MAI samples.
  MAI rendering sends only the original sample sentences to Azure and incurs
  charges. Reference clips are measured locally, not uploaded.
- Reference clips you are entitled to use, kept outside the repository.
  Do not commit or share other people's recordings without permission.

Use the filename prefixes in
[`roles.example.json`](voice-match/roles.example.json), or supply your own
roles file with `--roles`. Clips must be directly inside the chosen folder;
the tool does not search subfolders. Supported extensions are `.mp3`, `.wav`,
`.flac`, `.ogg`, and `.m4a`; decoding support depends on the local setup.

```sh
npm run build
npm run voices:samples -- --kokoro --mai
npm run voices:match -- --clips "/path/to/reference-clips"
```

In PowerShell, use `npm.cmd` for commands with `--` arguments.
To compare just one service, render it with only `--kokoro` or `--mai` and
use a samples folder containing only that service. Matching reads every
available service folder, regardless of which one was rendered most recently.

Generated samples are saved in `~/.picard-code/voice-match/samples/`.
Existing sample files are reused, so changed sentences or speaking settings
need a fresh output folder to avoid comparing stale audio. Rendering supports
`--output`, and matching supports `--samples`.

The default matching command **overwrites the repository's comparison report**.
For an exploratory run, keep the output outside the repository:

```sh
npm run voices:match -- --clips "/path/to/reference-clips" --report "$HOME/.picard-code/voice-match/comparison.json"
```

The listening page is `~/.picard-code/voice-match/listen.html`. Open it locally
to hear the assigned officer voice first, followed by allowed alternatives.
Comparison roles show their raw rankings. Its audio links expect a sibling
`samples/` folder; keep that layout if you use custom paths.

The first matching run downloads roughly 2.5 GB of packages and models.
Rendering and matching can take time. MAI rendering prints the pending
character count and refuses work above `--max-characters` (60,000 by default);
it reuses existing samples without another request. Inspect the report's
`models` section to see which models actually contributed before relying on
a new result. Do not commit local audio, downloaded models, or settings.

# Community code of conduct

Picard Code welcomes people of all backgrounds and experience levels.
Treat contributors, users, and maintainers with respect. This applies to issues,
pull requests, Discussions, and other spaces representing the project.

## Working together

- Be patient, considerate, and clear. Critique ideas and code, not people.
- Welcome questions and constructive feedback. Accept corrections gracefully.
- Respect privacy, personal boundaries, and other people's creative work.
- Keep discussions relevant and make room for different experiences.

Harassment, discrimination, threats, sexualized attention, personal attacks,
and publishing someone else's private information are not acceptable.

## Reporting and moderation

For non-sensitive project conduct concerns, contact the maintainer,
[@sbroenne](https://github.com/sbroenne), in the affected GitHub thread.
Do not post private information to make a report. For harassment, threats, or
sensitive abuse, use [GitHub's private abuse reporting tools](https://docs.github.com/en/communities/maintaining-your-safety-on-github/reporting-abuse-or-spam).
The project does not offer a separate private messaging inbox.

The maintainer may edit or remove disruptive content, close discussions, or
restrict participation. Responses should be proportionate: clarification or a
warning for minor problems, and temporary or permanent exclusion for serious
or repeated harm. Reports are considered as availability permits; no response
deadline is promised.

This policy follows the welcoming principles of the
[Contributor Covenant](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/) and uses original
wording for this project's reporting arrangements.

# Help shape the computer

Picard Code is an unofficial tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart and Captain
Jean-Luc Picard. You speak to an original ship-computer-style interface, and
OpenCode does the coding. Contributions are welcome, including ideas, tests,
research, and documentation, not just code.

## Where help matters most

**The computer's character.** Help it give calm, concise, useful spoken answers,
understand follow-ups and corrections, pronounce technical names, and choose
comfortable timing. The user is Captain Picard; the computer says "Captain"
occasionally, not in every reply. Use original examples, not show dialogue.
Character should come from precision and delivery, not repeated catchphrases
or invented ship status.

**More listening and speaking models.** Add independently selectable services,
especially local options. Explain installation, model licenses, hardware needs,
data destinations, and charges. Cancellation and service errors must work;
never switch silently to another service. See `src/server/speech-types.ts`,
`src/server/speech.ts`, and the existing Azure, Nemotron and Kokoro
implementations. Nemotron is the local listener. Saved Whisper installations
upgrade automatically, saving only after the replacement starts successfully;
keep their speaking choice and old downloaded files. Other service changes
need an explicit choice. Azure speech stays under Advanced setup.

Other useful contributions:

- Accessible desktop controls: keyboard use, screen readers, readable text,
  reduced motion, and clear listening states.
- Real microphone testing beyond the owner's own Windows and macOS setups:
  other accents, quiet speech, echo, headphones, room noise, pauses,
  "Computer", follow-ups, and returning to standing by.
- Linux installation and troubleshooting; Windows and macOS are in regular use.
- Reliable startup, shutdown, reconnection, and listening/playback transitions.
- Measured improvements in response time and local resource use.

## Keep the spirit

Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md), the single source of development rules, before
changing code. [PRODUCT.md](PRODUCT.md) and [DESIGN.md](DESIGN.md) describe the
experience. The app is voice-only and designed for a computer screen:
typed requests, a phone app, and unrelated general-assistant features are
outside the current direction.

Use plain English and the TNG terms listed in AGENTS.md: Captain's log,
log entry, Stardate, and Standing by. Keep exact errors and the user's words.
The computer must not claim something happened before the result arrives.
Do not add copied franchise artwork, recordings, show dialogue, or performer
voice cloning.

Keep secrets, personal conversations, downloaded models, and local settings
out of changes, screenshots, and reports. Use original generated test phrases
or samples you have permission to share. Do not submit recordings of other
people without their informed permission.

## Start with an idea or a small task

Look at [help wanted issues](https://github.com/sbroenne/picard-code/labels/help%20wanted)
and [good first issues](https://github.com/sbroenne/picard-code/labels/good%20first%20issue).
Use the character or speech proposal form for a new direction; use
[Discussions](https://github.com/sbroenne/picard-code/discussions) for open-ended
ideas and questions. Discuss a large change before investing in it. A feature
request is not a promise that it will be accepted.

For bugs, include reproduction steps, expected and actual behavior, operating
system, browser, and selected services. Do not post keys, temporary launch
addresses, or private project files. Use [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) for
sensitive security reports.

## Make and check a change

Fork the repository, create a branch, and follow
[Run from source](README.md#run-from-source). Use your own OpenCode sign-in and speech resources.
OpenCode 2 is required; `npm start` installs the tested copy and builds the app
before launching.

Dependency installs use the npm registry already configured on your computer.
Keep the project's `.npmrc` setting `omit-lockfile-registry-resolved=true`:
it leaves registry download addresses out of `package-lock.json`, while
keeping exact versions and integrity checks. Update the lockfile with npm,
not by deleting fields by hand, and preserve source addresses for dependencies
that do not come from a registry. Do not change personal or global npm settings
to work around an installation failure. After dependency changes, run `npm ci`.
Vite and its compatible Rolldown override are pinned to versions available
through the approved feed; check both compatibility and download availability
before updating them.

Before each commit, choose the checks that match the change.
For changes only to documentation, the project website (`site/`),
development-only tools (`tools/`), or `browser-tests/site.spec.ts`, run:

```sh
npx playwright test browser-tests/site.spec.ts
```

This checks desktop and phone layouts and documentation links without building
or testing the app. For tool code changes, also run the checks that cover the
changed tool. Tools are not shipped with the app and do not need the full app
checks unless the change also touches app code, shared dependencies, setup
scripts or check configuration. Release note text can accompany these changes.

For app code, dependencies, setup scripts, check configuration, or any other
files, run the full checks:

```sh
npm run check
npm run build
npm test
npx playwright test
```

Changes to the changed-file rules also need
`node --test .github/scripts/check-scope.test.mjs`.
GitHub follows the same split; manual runs always use full checks.
See [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md#checks) for the rules.

Real local speech checks are an additional, narrow selection, not part of
every full check. Relevant local speech/setup changes run Nemotron, Kokoro
and Smart Turn on GitHub-hosted Mac, Ubuntu and Windows computers. Browser
capture/detection changes select focused real Chromium/Silero checks on
Mac and Windows; Ubuntu already runs them in the browser suite.
Unrelated dependency updates, release versions, documentation, styling and
ordinary reply wording do not select those extra jobs. Dependency selection
compares the relevant resolved packages, not just whether a lockfile changed.
See [the exact selection rules](.github/scripts/speech-scope.mjs) and
[the cache and manual-run guide](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md#which-github-checks-run-real-speech).
Changing those rules also requires `node --test .github/scripts/*.test.mjs`.

The complete pull request determines the selection. Adding documentation to
a PR that still contains speech changes reruns its selected speech checks.
Only model downloads are cached, never test results. Pushes to main do not
repeat the extra jobs. Manual runs use no extra speech jobs unless
**speech-checks** explicitly selects **local**, **browser** or **all**.

If Chromium is missing, run `npx playwright install chromium`. Windows users
should use `npm.cmd` for commands with `--` arguments.

These checks use a test stand-in for OpenCode and generated audio. When changing
models, speech, or conversation behavior, also run the matching real checks in the
[developer guide](docs/DEVELOPMENT.md#real-service-checks). They can require your own sign-in,
model downloads, or paid Azure/model requests. Report exactly what ran and what
could not; never submit credentials to CI.

Keep changes focused and update related documentation. In a pull request,
explain the user-facing difference and the checks you ran.
Screenshots of stand-ins must be labeled. New speech services need license,
data-flow, setup, error, and cancellation documentation. To change an
officer's voice, or add voices from a new speech service, measure them with
`tools/voice-match` as described in
[docs/research/bridge-crew-voices.md](docs/research/bridge-crew-voices.md#speaking-voices).

### Release notes

If people using Picard Code will notice your change, add a release note: run
`npx changeset`, choose **patch**, and write one or two plain sentences about
what changed for them. Commit the new file in `.changeset/` with your change.
**Minor** is kept for a major redesign the maintainer chooses; never choose
**major**. Changes only to tests, checks or contributor docs need no note.
The release notes link your pull request and thank you by name.

## Review and AI assistance

Copilot and other coding tools are welcome. Read their changes yourself and
take responsibility for correctness, licenses, and honest evidence. Copilot
review helps find problems; it does not replace maintainer judgment.

The maintainer reviews pull requests with the [Ponytail](https://github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail)
review skill in `.github/skills/ponytail-review`. It checks that a change is
correct, safe, tested, and no bigger than it needs to be. Copilot code review
on GitHub can use it. If your coding tool reads skills, ask it for a
`ponytail-review` of your branch before opening the pull request.
The maintainer decides what fits the project and merges manually.

Once a week, the Code Simplifier (`.github/workflows/code-simplifier.md`, from
the public [Agentics](https://github.com/githubnext/agentics) library) reads
the code merged in the past week. It may open one small draft pull request
titled `[code-simplifier]`. It must not change anything users see or hear,
and it leaves speech, conversation, crew, tribute and safety code alone.
Review it like any other pull request. Unmerged ones close after a week; the
generated `agentics-maintenance.yml` workflow checks for them every day.
To change it, edit the `.md` file and run `gh aw compile` to regenerate the
matching `.lock.yml` and the maintenance workflow; `gh aw update` brings in
changes from the library.

The owner sets it up once:

1. **AI sign-in.** Create a
   [fine-grained personal access token](https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new?name=Picard+Code+Code+Simplifier&description=Copilot+requests+for+the+Code+Simplifier+workflow&expires_in=90&user_copilot_requests=read)
   owned by your account. Give it only the **Copilot requests** account
   permission, no repository permissions, and an expiry date. Replace it
   before it expires. Its runs use your Copilot requests. Save it with
   `gh secret set COPILOT_GITHUB_TOKEN`, which asks for the value. gh-aw
   cannot use a GitHub App for this. The token-free option needs an
   organization's Copilot plan, which a personal repository does not have.
2. **GitHub App for the pull request.** It creates the draft pull request, so
   the required checks start, using a short-lived token for each run.
   [Register a private app](https://github.com/settings/apps/new?name=Picard+Code+workflows&url=https://github.com/sbroenne/picard-code&public=false&webhook_active=false&checks=read&contents=write&issues=write&pull_requests=write)
   with only these repository permissions: Checks read, Contents read and
   write, Issues read and write, and Pull requests read and write. Leave the
   webhook off. Install it on this repository only. Save its Client ID with
   `gh variable set GH_AW_APP_CLIENT_ID --body "<client id>"`, generate a
   private key, save it with
   `gh secret set GH_AW_APP_PRIVATE_KEY < path/to/key.pem`, then delete the
   downloaded key file. Without the App, runs still report failures and may
   open the pull request, but its checks do not start on their own.

## Platform

## Product Purpose

A tribute to Sir Patrick Stewart and Captain Jean-Luc Picard, made with deep
respect and gratitude. You give spoken orders as Captain Picard: questions,
writing, research, planning and code. OpenCode carries out the work through a
local browser interface with an original computer-display design inspired by
Star Trek: The Next Generation.

## Operating Context

Runs locally on Windows, Apple silicon macOS, and Linux. Intel Macs are not
supported. Node.js 24 or newer is required; OpenCode 2 is included or reused
when already installed. The terminal's current folder is the default Project;
the Captain can choose another folder and connect an AI provider through
OpenCode. Any model provider OpenCode supports can be used.

## Capabilities and Constraints

The app keeps log entries in Captain's log, shows live replies, uses the
selected Project as context, and displays real OpenCode approval requests.
Credentials stay out of the browser. Services listen locally and must reject
requests from unrelated websites. People run it with `npx picard-code`, which
uses an installed OpenCode 2 or its own copy and prepares the selected speech
services.

Spoken requests are the only input; there is no typing fallback. The app is
designed for a computer screen, not a phone. The microphone switches on when
speech is ready and the Captain opens a channel on first start-up, subject to
browser permission and sound restrictions.
"Computer" addresses the computer; follow-ups need no prefix until the Captain
returns to Standing by. Requests continue the Current log entry unless the
Captain explicitly starts a new one. End-of-speech detection sends requests
without routine transcript review or a Send step. Brief spoken answers accompany
full written results. Follow-ups keep context; microphone off, Stop speaking,
and Belay that (stop work) have separate meanings. Decisions remain deliberate.
Listening remains available during spoken replies so "Computer" can interrupt
playback without stopping work. Stop speaking also stops playback; Belay that
stops work. Video playback, computer sounds and open Ship's systems panels
pause listening. New work requests heard while work or a decision is pending
are not sent; answers to a pending question still use its own choices.

Listening and speaking share small, separate interfaces. Real CPU Nemotron
listening and Kokoro speaking are the default, so anyone can run Picard Code
without a cloud account. Whisper is retired; saved installations automatically
prepare Nemotron, keeping their speaking choice and saving only after startup.
Preparation shows real steps, not an invented percentage, and failures offer retry.
Nemotron shows words during speech, but only a complete request is sent.
The supported MAI live listening and prebuilt MAI
speaking services can be chosen instead, each side on its own.
Azure listening receives detected speech before deciding whether "Computer"
was said, including speech not meant for the model. Processing can occur
outside Europe. Standing by still listens; microphone off stops capture.
Keys remain in local server memory;
connection settings contain no secrets. Reuse suitable resources on the
explicitly approved subscription without changing spending limits or access.

Both setups use the same spoken exchange and deliberate decisions, with
no silent fallback. Local audio processing needs no Azure credentials;
recognized coding requests still go to the chosen model.

Any model provider OpenCode supports can be used, such as GitHub Copilot,
Anthropic, OpenAI or a local model. Sign-ins go through OpenCode's own flow and
stay with OpenCode; credentials from other tools must not be extracted.
Before listening starts, an AI model must be confirmed. Begin start-up confirms
a default the Captain already set in OpenCode; otherwise the Captain chooses
and confirms a model. Picard Code never chooses a replacement on its own.
Recommend the most capable model available for the best experience, with
clear cost and speed considerations. Remember the choice on this computer
across Projects and restarts, separately from OpenCode's default. If it becomes
unavailable, ask for another choice rather than switching models automatically.

## Brand Commitments

Picard Code. Plain English. Black background, peach, orange, and lilac panels,
rounded side bars, and readable conversation text. No copied franchise assets
or implied endorsement.

The computer's writing should be brief, precise, and neutral. Use original
phrasing, truthful acknowledgments, explicit uncertainty, and useful errors.
No voice cloning, show dialogue, or recordings in the repository. Four short
computer sounds are downloaded separately from the npm package and checked
automatically at startup. Their attribution and permission limits are in
[THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md); they accompany, never replace,
the visible and spoken explanation. No fictional ship status, repetitive
catchphrases, or claims that work succeeded before the real result arrives.

The computer uses fixed ready-made voices: Kokoro Alloy (`af_alloy`) and
Azure MAI Iris (`en-US-Iris`, neutral style). Each bridge officer has a separate
fixed voice. There is no voice-selection control; listening and speaking
services remain independently selectable. The choices are measured comparisons,
not performer clones or claims of authenticity.

The user is always Captain Jean-Luc Picard, labeled "Picard" on screen.
The computer says "Captain" occasionally. Use the plain TNG terms in AGENTS.md:

# Reporting a security problem

Picard Code is an early source release. Only the current `main` branch receives
fixes; there are no supported older release branches.

Please use [GitHub's private vulnerability reporting](https://github.com/sbroenne/picard-code/security/advisories/new).
Do not open a public issue with credentials, private project content, or
instructions that would expose other users. If the private reporting form is
unavailable, start a [discussion](https://github.com/sbroenne/picard-code/discussions)
that only asks the maintainer for a private way to report a security problem,
with no details.

Include the affected commit, operating system, browser, reproduction steps,
expected and actual behavior, and impact. Use a minimal example containing no
secrets or other people's data. Do not test against another person's computer,
account, project, or cloud resource.

The maintainer reviews reports as availability permits; no response time or
paid support is promised. Coordinate public disclosure after a fix is available.

Never attach Azure keys, provider credentials, your speech settings file
(`~/.picard-code/speech.json`, or the older `.picard-speech.json`), a complete
launch address with its temporary key, personal log entries, or project files
you cannot share. Remove sensitive information from screenshots and logs.
If a real credential has been exposed, revoke or rotate it with its provider;
deleting a GitHub comment alone does not make it safe again.

## Limits

The app listens on `127.0.0.1`; it is not designed to be served publicly.
The local protections do not defend against a malicious program already
running on the same computer. OpenCode owns its model connections and
permission rules. Selected hosted providers receive project content; Azure
listening receives detected speech even before "Computer" is recognized.
Questions about Picard or Patrick Stewart fetch two fixed Wikipedia articles;
only the article titles are sent, never your words or project content.
Read README's data-flow explanation before use.

The GitHub Pages website is a static introduction, not a running app.

# Developing Picard Code

Read [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md) for the project rules and
[CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) for contribution and review guidance.
Follow [Run from source](../README.md#run-from-source) to clone, install and
build the app. Use your own OpenCode sign-in and speech resources.

## Live updates while developing

Use `npm run dev` instead of `npm start`. For Azure MAI on both sides, run
`npm run dev -- --listening mai --speaking mai`. Vite updates browser code
and styles automatically; changes to the page itself reload it. Restart the
command after changing server code. This development mode stays on
`127.0.0.1`, uses the real app and its normal sign-in checks, and does not
change the normal launch or your saved speech choices.
If the browser cannot open, the servers keep running so you can open the
printed live-updates address yourself. Windows shutdown stops the app's
child processes too.
After building, `node --test tools/dev.test.mjs tools/dev-server.test.mjs`
checks launcher failures and shutdown, live style updates and the development
server's local connection checks.

In PowerShell, use `npm.cmd` for commands with `--` options; some npm
PowerShell wrappers otherwise drop the `--`.

## Speech services

The shared interfaces are in `src/server/speech-types.ts`. A listener accepts
one channel of signed little-endian 16-bit audio at 16,000 samples per second,
reports understood words, and commits a turn on request. A speaker streams
the same audio format at 24,000 samples per second. Both receive a cancellation
signal; `close()` releases owned workers. Selection happens in
`src/server/speech.ts`, without changes to the browser's conversation controls.
See [third-party notices](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md) before redistributing local
dependencies or downloaded models.

Conversation instructions live in `src/server/instructions.ts` and are sent
with every request. Speech wording lives in `src/shared/speech.ts`.

## Checks

For changes only to documentation or the project website, use
`npx playwright test browser-tests/site.spec.ts`. It checks website layouts
and documentation links without building the app. App, dependency, setup and
check configuration changes still need full checks. The complete rules,
including development-only tools, are in [AGENTS.md](../AGENTS.md#checks)
and [CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md#make-and-check-a-change).

```sh
npm run check
npm run build
npm test
npx playwright test
```

`check` finds likely mistakes and unused code with oxlint, then checks the
types of the server and browser code. Build before running server tests:
they run the compiled files in `dist/`.

### Which GitHub checks run real speech

Real speech checks are separate from the normal app checks. They use
GitHub-hosted Apple silicon macOS, Ubuntu x64 and Windows x64 computers;
there are no self-hosted runners and no paid AI-provider or Azure requests.

| What the pull request changes | Extra checks |
| --- | --- |
| Local speech services, workers, setup, fixed voices or real-check inputs | Real Nemotron listening, Kokoro speaking and Smart Turn pause predictions on all three systems |
| Browser speech capture, Silero detection, utterance timing or their focused tests | Real Chromium/Silero checks on Mac and Windows, alongside Ubuntu's existing browser suite; no large speech downloads |
| Relevant resolved npm dependencies or their dependencies, Node requirements, or the corresponding check's runtime/build settings | Only the affected checks |
| Documentation, website, styling, ordinary reply wording, unrelated app work, unrelated dependency updates or release-version-only edits | No extra real speech checks |

The exact file lists and dependency comparisons are in
[speech-scope.mjs](../.github/scripts/speech-scope.mjs). Utterance timing is kept
separate from reply formatting so wording edits do not select model checks.
General workflow edits run the fast workflow tests; editing a speech
workflow itself selects its real checks.

Selection uses the complete pull request, not just its latest commit.
If a pull request contains speech changes, a later README-only commit still
reruns the selected speech checks. Passing test results are never cached.
The existing required checks reject failed, cancelled or unexpectedly skipped
speech checks. Pushes to main do not automatically repeat these extra checks.

Only the downloaded model files and their notices are cached. Every selected
run prepares the software afresh, verifies the files' checksums and executes
the models. Cache misses or eviction require another download.
GitHub keeps pull-request caches separate, so new pull requests can reuse a
cache from main but cannot use another pull request's cache.
To seed those shared caches, or to check speech manually, run **Project checks**
from GitHub Actions on main with **speech-checks: all**. Choose **local** for
Nemotron/Kokoro/Smart Turn, **browser** for focused browser detection, or
**none** (the default) for the existing checks only.
This input does not change saved speech choices or request a release.

Silero's model runs in browser WebAssembly; Smart Turn's model runs in the
local Python worker. Their model files are portable, but running them on
each system checks the actual browser and local software there.
These checks use original generated audio, not a physical microphone.
They do not establish Safari/Firefox behaviour, room-echo handling or a full
real AI-provider conversation.

### What the checks cover

The server and browser tests use a clearly labeled local test server that follows
OpenCode 2's connection format, through Picard Code's own OpenCode client. They cover live replies, saved
log entries, approvals, questions, folder boundaries, browser request
protection, safe text rendering, and the desktop layout. They do not claim
to have called a real model or executed a shell command. Speech tests use an
artificial browser microphone and simulated speakers, with an explicitly separate speech test service
to check automatic turns, follow-up context, listening during playback,
deliberate approvals, and separate stopping controls. They also use silent
stand-in sound files to check that each computer sound plays once at the right
moment, never while listening, and not for answers to questions or cancelled work.

The reload checks deliberately slow the startup stand-in sound on both click
and keyboard routes. They wait for its actual playback end and the 200 ms
echo guard before sending the generated microphone phrase. A Listening label
alone does not mean the sound has finished. Keep this overlap in the normal
pull-request suite so a faster earlier run cannot hide the test's timing mistake.

If Playwright reports a missing browser, run `npx playwright install chromium`
and repeat the browser checks.

## Reply rendering checks

`browser-tests/outputs.spec.ts` uses original diagrams, generated PDF/Office
files and silent audio, with a labelled OpenCode stand-in. It checks the actual
decimal chart coordinates, several Mermaid families, maths, code colouring,
work errors and partial results, document viewers, streamed/saved update order,
reopening, a second page, microphone restarts and preview cancellation.
`src/tests/app.test.ts` checks reply ownership, Project containment, inline
attachments, file-size limits and Office archive expansion, including forged
sizes. Build before running the compiled server tests.

The installed OpenCode 2.2.0 connection was checked against its real local API.
The display inventory was compared with OpenCode's 2.2.5 browser/schema sources
at `21eaa626a37f77d7a8d80fa01997fa7d52506c97`: text/reasoning, all four tool
states, text/file tool content (including failed content), shell reports,
human-readable instruction notices, context summaries and the file kinds listed
in the [user guide](USER_GUIDE.md#graphs-documents-and-work-results).
Model/officer/Project selection entries remain settings changes, not spoken
answers; private system instructions and provider replay metadata are not
forwarded for display.

This is not a promise to host arbitrary future OpenCode plugins. Heavy viewers
load on demand. Mermaid, maths and code use Pele, KaTeX and Pierre Highlights;
PDF uses PDF.js, DOCX uses docx-preview, and XLSX/PPTX use BetterOffice. A small
DOM adapter avoids importing OpenCode's private Solid application and contexts.
The build copies renderer licenses and available notices into
`web-dist/renderer-notices.txt`; keep that file in the shipped package.

## Real service checks

Build first. Confirm a current-generation model with
`npm run opencode -- models` before choosing a model for a check.
Never change the owner's saved model or speech choices to run a check.
Some checks need model downloads, a signed-in provider or paid Azure services.
Report exactly what ran and what could not run.

```sh
npm run test:live
npm run test:speech:live
npm run test:speech:local
npm run test:conversation:live
npm.cmd run test:conversation:live -- --local --model provider/model
npm.cmd run test:conversation:live -- --local --interrupt --model provider/model
npm.cmd run test:conversation:live -- --local --quiet-interrupt --model provider/model
npm.cmd run test:crew:live -- --model provider/model
npm.cmd run test:behavior:live -- --model provider/model
```

The `npm.cmd` examples are for Windows. On macOS or Linux, use `npm`.
Replace `provider/model` with an available current-generation model.

### OpenCode connection

`test:live` starts **real OpenCode**, checks its health, project folder, saved
log entry, live updates, and approval/question requests, then removes its
own check log entry and shuts its server down. It does not make a paid model
request. A real model reply needs a signed-in provider.

### Listening and speaking

`test:speech:live` makes small, chargeable requests to the configured
**real Azure** services. It synthesizes an original short test phrase and sends the
generated audio through MAI's live listening connection, checking both final
words and live word updates. It also speaks a long, number-heavy answer
piece by piece at the slowest speed, as the app does, so each piece stays
under the service's audio limit. It does not capture your microphone or call
an AI model.

`test:speech:local` performs real CPU Kokoro synthesis and Nemotron recognition. It feeds audio
at microphone pace, checks live Nemotron words before commit, names and
negations, and listening/speaking cancellation followed by fresh listening.
It also asks the real Smart Turn worker to distinguish a complete request
from an unfinished one, cancels a prediction and checks a fresh prediction.
It speaks a long, number-heavy answer piece by piece at the slowest speed,
so each piece stays under Kokoro's audio limit. It saves an original sample under `.picard-voice/samples` and neither reads
nor changes saved speech choices. These short examples do not establish
general recognition or pause-detection accuracy. Generated speech does not
test a physical microphone.

### Complete spoken requests and replies

`test:conversation:live` checks the complete real MAI browser path using
generated microphone audio, OpenCode, a real model from your signed-in provider, saved
messages, live text updates, and real spoken playback. `--local` checks the
same path with Nemotron and Kokoro. Both explicitly confirm
their test model using a throwaway settings file.
Add `--model provider/model` to choose a particular available model for the
check. This does not change your saved Picard Code model or speech choices.
Both paths exercise the real local completion model through the browser's
captured audio and confirm that a pause was checked before submission.
Prepare speech first as described in [Natural pauses](USER_GUIDE.md#natural-pauses).
Add `--interrupt` to play a generated request into the browser's capture path
while a real spoken answer is playing. It checks that playback stops, the
new request keeps its name and negation, and no stop-work request is sent.
This tests overlapping speech, not a physical microphone or speaker echo.
Use `--quiet-interrupt` instead to check a softer request spoken while an
answer is playing. The voice detector decides by how speech sounds, not by
volume alone, so softer speech can still start listening.
These checks make real model requests;
the MAI variant also makes chargeable Azure requests. Earlier versions of both
passed on the Windows development machine before the OpenCode 2 migration;
those results do not verify the current version. They remove their own check log entries and
save screenshots and generated audio in the ignored samples folder.

### Bridge crew

`test:crew:live` checks real officer replies and a few measurable voice
habits (no exclamation marks, Data without contractions, Worf brief), "Make it
so" carrying out an officer's own proposal, an unclear "Make it so" answered
with a request for clarification, a quick fact, an explanation and a piece of
writing kept by the computer, requests needing an officer's judgment handed to
the right officer without naming them (including misheard names), and real
briefings with real officer calls and Number One calling officers when
explicitly asked to organise their work. It also checks that a ban on tools
or officer calls is respected and Worf does not know a hypothetical
post-death event, even when asked to use later archives. It cannot judge whether an
officer sounds right; that needs you. Add `-- --show-replies` to print the six
generated officer replies for review. The check makes model requests, may incur
provider charges, and never answers an approval itself.
The check requires an explicit model choice and does not change your saved choice.

### Follow-ups and approvals

`test:behavior:live` holds a six-turn log entry with a real model from your signed-in
provider through Picard Code's own local interface, in a temporary project
outside this repository. It checks a short investigation, a follow-up, a
correction, "show me", OpenCode's real question with a spoken-style answer,
and a refused command approval that must not run. It writes the full exchange
to `.picard-voice/samples/behavior-transcript.md`. Model wording varies; the
check verifies behavior, not exact words.
The check requires an explicit model choice and does not change your saved choice.

- **Protect main** (Settings → Rules): changes need a pull request, squash
